pitch_detail.notes: Slab with very little protection and a slabby crux, so commit; reversing it would be unpleasant. Reach a pair of flakes and work them with jams, laybacks or stemming through a second hard section. The left flake eases into a gentle ramp that serves as a good belay. Starts at the far east end of the face, where the green lichen reaches highest.

Continue up the ramp, then up a clean rounded dihedral leading left before stepping right onto the slab. Head for the notch above and right with one exposed slab move, ending at a fine belay in the notch. The East Buttress starts below and to the right of it.

review.changed: Wrote both pitches. Only pitch 1 has a stated grade; no lengths. No rappel table (descent is a scramble or link-up).

pitch_detail.notes: Long full-rack pitch, and the longest on the route (the rest are 30 m or less). Bouldery moves on the smallest cams lead into a laser-cut splitter, then flared jams and a field of mid-size cracks, a hard section, a pumpy layback on a single run of cams, and a gear-protected boulder problem. Shallow placements near the top want totems; other brands may rip. Save a blue totem for the end. Rappelling this pitch takes a rope of at least 70 m.

Face climbing up and to the right of the belay with 3 bolts, then easy flakes with one more bolt and a few pieces to an overlap. A bolt there, then a punchy crux with another bolt, brings you under a big flake. Layback it with two bolts and a piece or two, finishing on juggy flakes. Single rack from black totem to #2.

Committing gear-protected moves reach a high first bolt, then hollow flakes go past another bolt to an undercling flake. Layback its left side past gear to a bolt, boulder right along a seam (about V4) to a big stand-up, clip, then a difficult, committing boulder problem (about V6) onto a layback flake. A strenuous clip is necessary; one more bolt leads to the anchor. With the full rack and extra #0.5 and #0.75 cams it can be linked with the next pitch.

Leave the belay going up and right on face moves with two bolts, then curve back left into an odd crack system. Gear is available as you go, and several cruxes demand thoughtful, gear-protected climbing. Double rack from 0.1 to #0.75 plus offset wires.

The route's crux. Climb to a high first bolt, then a sustained overhanging stretch of granite with poor footholds and many cruxes, closer to limestone-style face climbing. A couple of fair rests exist but only help if you climb efficiently. Bolted, so take 11 draws; an easier runout comes near the end.

Commit to moves along a rail heading straight left, with two bolts and a piece or two. A runout section follows; set nested gear and climb into a crack and groove. Where the crack ends in a bottoming groove, put in solid gear (a totem is ideal), then reach up and left past a bolt and finish back right onto a good ledge.

Final pitch is no easy topout: a punchy left-leaning hanging corner with 5 bolts and a few placements. Bring small and micro cams for the last moves. It is short and the ledge is always close, so the belayer should stay attentive. Rappel from here, or scramble left along an exposed ramp to the summit, staying roped.

review.changed: Wrote pitches 1 to 7 with stated grades. Left out the easy ledgy approach 'pitch 0'. No rappel table: only the pitch 1 rope-length requirement and 'rappel from the top' are given.

pitch_detail.notes: In good conditions this is a run of undulating rampy steps, alternating between solid horizontal edges, frozen moss and turf, and ice or neve sticks. Three widely spaced bolts, all on the groove's left side, can be supplemented with several pieces. Belay on a small, comfortable ledge at the foot of the first steep rock.

Three distinct steps lead to the top, each with engaging footwork. Seven bolts, on both left and right sides, plus a few pieces protect it. Belayers should be careful with slack at the start of the third step, since the ledge there is large. Belay and rappel from another offset anchor with rings. Short screws help in icy conditions.

rappel_detail.anchor: offset multipitch anchor with rap rings
rappel_detail.notes: Rappel back to the pitch 1 belay.
Rappel to the ground. A single 80 m rope could descend in one go with some stretch and easy downclimbing, though a walk-off is not advised.

review.changed: Wrote 2 pitches and a 2-station rappel table (no per-rappel lengths stated).
review.other_findings: Stored descent_text is null; text says rappel the route (walk-off possible but not advised).

pitch_detail.notes: Begin with a finger crack rising from an open pod. Pass a ledge, follow cracks angling left to a second ledge, and scramble to a third. A short splitter hand crack leads to an arete; round it and cross the gully to a broad belay shelf on the formation's face.

Probably shared with other routes that reach this point from the front apron of Toe 2. Go straight up blocky ground to twin cracks and a cruxy offwidth. Exit the wide part, pass a tree, and romp up very loose fourth-class ground to the next belay.

About 90 percent easy fourth-class ridge scramble up to a final slab block just below the summit. Trend around its right side but take the crack that splits the slab rather than the easiest line, with a few solid hand jams and a wide, low-angle crack. Shimmy to the summit ridge and stop just under the top. This pitch may also be shared with other routes.

review.changed: Wrote 3 pitches. No rappel table: the descent is a scramble with one final tree rappel.

pitch_detail.notes: Crack-filled slabs lead toward a chimney and a left-facing corner. Belay on a ledge.
Leave the chimney by going up and right on good edges and jugs to a nice crack. Above it, go up and left through a squeeze to a large sloping ledge for the belay. Loose rock here.
Short move of the belay up and left, crossing onto the exposed face to a great stance.
Obvious face on good jugs with a well-protected crack. Views of Elephant's Perch from the top.

review.changed: Wrote 4 pitches with stated grades; lengths only for pitches 1, 3 and 4. No rappel table (descent is the standard one for the formation).

pitch_detail.notes: Several variations exist. From the grass meadow go up and left to another ledge under a small groove, climb balancy moves directly up to a ramp leaning left, follow it left, then mantel to the next ramp and continue easily to a roomy ledge. Some blue tat on a nut sits to the right. Build a belay from hand-size gear in a corner. Alternatively, move further left for a 5.6 offwidth, or bushwhack around.

Step up to the next ledge, then ascend a gentle corner leaning up and left, keeping to the left of the wet gully, on slabs to a brushy terrace. A faint trail through the shrubs leads to the foot of a leftward undercling flake, where you belay.

Follow the undercling flake up and left; good feet make it easier than it looks. Pull onto a ledge. The original line continues left past a huge block; the right variation makes a tricky move right into a burly layback flake (a stuck 0.5 Z4 was there in 2024), then physical moves up and right to a stance and one more tricky move onto the right-trending ledge system. Belay on solid rock.
A ramp trending right gives airy exposure as it passes under a big corner. Step round the corner and belay on a grassy ledge under a water-streaked gully.

Very long, a rope stretcher even on a 70 m depending on the belay you pick. Easy ground up the gully gives way to a slab, where the climbing changes from steep corners and cracks to low-angle, open slabs with shallow features. Runout, with loose rock, to a broken corner facing left. Belay on solid rock at its top. The corner passed on the pitch 4 ramp seems to join the line and might offer better climbing.

Two finishes. Left finish: step off the belay to the left and romp up runout slabs to a headwall, place gear, then do the crux moves up and left onto a ledge, continue up and left toward a bushy terrace and straight up easier ground to where fifth-class climbing ends. The right finish is said to step right to a steep headwall, then often-wet lower-angle slabs and short twin cracks to the top, also 5.8 PG13.

review.changed: Wrote 6 pitches with stated grades; no lengths. No rappel table (descent is a long walk-off).
review.other_findings: Stored length 335 m looks long for six pitches described mostly as moderate; not verified. Descent is a walk-off over Howe Peak.

pitch_detail.notes: Dirtiest of the three, with little protection. The first few moves can be wet after rain. Start right of a big oak that lost its top in a rockfall, go up left to a small dirty ledge, then up right through grass to the first belay ledge.

Exposed moves on mediocre rock. Go up left around the slight overhang above the belay to a featureless ramp, pull onto the exposed arete and keep climbing on edges toward the right. Belay by slinging two small trees.
Climb above the belay, right of the block, to the treehouse-like belay ledge, which has webbing and rap rings.

rappel_detail.notes: One rappel to the base using two 80 m ropes.

review.changed: Wrote 3 pitches; the lengths for pitches 1 and 2 are the text's own approximations (65 ft and 110 ft). One rappel entry.

pitch_detail.notes: Start on a few ledges leading to an open corner feature with gray rock to its right and a ramp to its left. Soon after the start, past a steep section, you hit the crux at a wide crack in the middle of the corner; it protects with big cams and may be wet. Continue up it, using the face for holds, shift up and right onto reddish rock (loose blocks here), follow the crack system past a big pod, and belay at the slight arete where a false summit appears. Save small cams for this anchor.

Most route-finding and most loose rock. Go up the gully above, keeping the previous belay to the right of the arete so the belayer is out of the fall line. Pick the hand crack on the left or the corner on the right, pass a very loose ledge, test every block, and place a big cam in the pod above. Move right below the ridge, then up to gain it. Belay with a slung horn and small cams.

Follow the gully with no protection and plenty of loose rock at 5.0 until a steep face, which takes good gear and has the crux, one 5.7 move. Rock tends to come loose here. Follow the arete and one more steep crack to the summit. Belay from a solid block slung past the stacked rocks.

review.changed: Wrote 3 pitches; lengths from feet (210, 200, 100). Only pitch 3 has a stated grade. No rappel table (walk-off).
review.other_findings: Stored grade 5.6 PG13, but the text names a single 5.7 move as the crux of the final pitch.

pitch_detail.notes: Begin on a thin broken crack system, passing the tree on its left. Beyond the tree is about 20 ft of excellent hand crack, then a lower-angle ramp with fewer protection options. Anchor in the crack below a bush.
Right of the bush, go up the loose gully; unpleasant but it reaches the walk-off. Anchor at the gully's end before it turns right.

review.changed: Wrote 2 pitches with lengths from 180 ft and 160 ft. No grades stated per pitch. No rappel table (walk-off).

pitch_detail.notes: Either WI3 ice or mossy M4 depending on conditions; the mixed version is runout. Protect with Spectres or ice screws.
Steep rock protected by cams (.3 to #1) and a permanent draw added to prevent a ground fall, then move onto the icicle and climb it to a tree at the top.

review.changed: Wrote 2 short pitches. Text is very brief: only pitch 1 gets a grade, no lengths, no anchors.
review.other_findings: Stored grade WI5-6 M7- is not matched by anything the text states (pitch 1 only WI3 or M4 R); pitch 2 is ungraded.

pitch_detail.notes: Climbs rock, moss and scraps of ice, and is only in shape when the ice at the top has formed. Protected by 6 bolts, 2 fixed pins and 1 to 3 screws. Take the left side of the top ice to a bolt out left, then low-angle ice to the anchor, which sits down and right of the next pitch's ice.
Two bolts come before you step onto the ice; then steep ice leads to the pitch's end.
Steep, well-protected drytooling up an inverted staircase, with mostly positive holds once you find them. Draws were left on all bolts as of 2024. It can easily be top-roped.

review.changed: Wrote 3 pitches with stated grades and lengths. No rappel table.

pitch_detail.notes: A bolt after good face holds, then wavy rock with small gear and three further bolts reaches a #2-3 crack that narrows to fingers. Pull through the finger crack to a small ledge, where a .3-.4 crack takes gear. Delicately pass an enormous, precariously stacked flake. Bolted anchor on a ledge behind the small tree.

Crimp, smear and use small feet past two bolts to a good stance, clip another bolt, pull onto a small ledge, and swing left around a bulge into a dihedral that is partly mossy. A fixed piton and finger cracks supply protection. Follow the dihedral to an obvious ledge with bolted anchors.

Traverse slightly left and mantel to a stance under a crack of splitter tips size. Clip the first bolt, then rely on the crack, the arete and smearing to reach the second. The crack widens a little to fingers; small cams and nuts protect a pull past a small roof to a jug and hand crack. Step left round the arete and clip a bolt, then follow a mossy dihedral with gear cracks, clip one more bolt, and work up a low-angle dihedral to belay bolts under the big roof.

review.changed: Wrote 3 pitches with stated grades and lengths; bolt counts are the ones the text lists in the pitch descriptions. No rappel table: the text says the route rappels on a single 70 m rope from bolted anchors but gives no station list.

pitch_detail.notes: Loose fourth-class climbing to reach the base of the gray slab.

Start from a gear belay in the corner system, move to the arete of the slab and follow its crest directly up; rock is solid near the crest. Protection is adequate, mostly smaller cams and nuts. Finish on top of the buttress crest, where good gear and slings on solid blocks make an anchor.

review.changed: Wrote 2 pitches; the slab pitch has no stated grade. No rappel table (walk-off).

pitch_detail.notes: Start as for two neighbouring routes, in the dihedral on the left of the wall. Climb it, then the first crack system straight up to a ledge at the foot of the massive arete, where a slung boulder serves as the anchor.
Go up and left from the anchor over a bolt-protected bulge, trend back right into a nice finger to hand crack, pull a roof and reach a tiny ledge on the arete with a bolted anchor.
Up left over a roof guarded by a bolt, then straight up with gear to a bolt line on a slab that trends right back to the arete. Hanging belay on bolts.
Head right onto the arete, clipping bolts and placing gear in a crack, and continue up a broken crack system with both gear and bolts to a big ledge with belay bolts.

Long pitch. Traverse right with a piece in the crack system below a neighbouring route, go right onto the face on bolts, then follow the arete to a mini ledge in a great position. Climb the crack system for about 40 ft, then traverse right toward the bolt line over a powerful roof (crux, on bolts), and finish up a hand crack to the top of the formation. Anchor on a big boulder. An easier 5.7 variation continues up the crack from the mini ledge to the top, aiming for a small left-facing dihedral, with an anchor or the tree's rappel sling.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel the route down to the top of pitch 2.
Rappel down to the first-pitch belay of the neighbouring route False Charge.
Last rappel to the ground, with some swinging involved.

review.changed: Wrote 5 pitches with stated grades; no lengths stated. Rappel table has 3 stations from the stated descent, without lengths.
review.other_findings: Stored descent_text matches. The text headline gives '5.11+ or 5.9+' (the latter if the pitch 5 variation is used).

pitch_detail.notes: Roughly 100 ft. Begin at a dihedral and cross a wide ledge to the right, or for an easier start cross small ledges leftward from further right on the wall to reach a small dihedral. Climb to below a small roof and belay on a ledge to the right.
Roughly 100 ft. Cross left beneath a small roof, then follow a small dihedral until you are 30 to 40 ft below a big roof that has steep crack systems on its right.

Roughly 150 ft. Traverse hard left about 50 ft off the belay, then go up cracks and broken ground to a small tree. A traverse starting 30 to 40 ft under the big roof protects easily; one from 15 to 20 ft under it is very runout, with a potential 100 ft pendulum.
Roughly 180 ft. Go right from the belay, then angle left across broken ground over a blunt prow to a small perch holding a dead tree, about 20 ft below a lichen-streaked roof.
Roughly 120 ft. Head left to a dihedral and continue to a ledge, go left along it and climb the arete to another ledge just right of a triangular roof 30 ft up.
Roughly 220 ft. More dihedrals and broken ground lead to a ledge with a couple of trees, right of and beneath a large dark brown roof about 100 ft up.
Roughly 250 ft, simul-climbed. Traverse hard left and slightly up on broken terrain and ledges to a spot directly below a huge dihedral system.

Roughly 350 ft. Climb a huge right-facing corner system, grassy at the start but becoming good climbing. It can be run out on the slabs or protected better nearer the corner. Belay at a tree 60 ft below big chockstones in a chimney.
Roughly 210 ft. A fully enclosed chimney choked with chockstones: climb up behind them, exit right onto a ledge, and continue up the dihedral to a tree belay.

Roughly 210 ft. Keep following the dihedral, through a roof, to a huge ledge system suitable for a bivy. About 300 ft of unroped scrambling follows, up and left on broken terrain to below a big clean wall.
Roughly 200 ft. Nice cracks to steep terrain, then a runout traverse right to a ledge below a big roof streaked with yellow lichen.
Roughly 230 ft. Up and left to an offwidth, then trend left and up on good crack systems to a tree ledge below a steep wall.

Roughly 230 ft. Take the main crack on the wall, through a small roof, to the top of the second tier, with the summit finally in view. Then unrope, descend and go hard right, and climb chossy gullies to a big set of ledges under a short wall.
Roughly 150 ft. A good crack system up to a chossy ledge, belaying under a huge yellow-lichen dihedral.
Roughly 180 ft. Up the yellow dihedral to a belay under a large offwidth flake.
Roughly 200 ft. Climb the offwidth flake, then up and slightly left on excellent rock to the summit.

review.changed: Wrote 16 pitches with stated grades. Lengths are in notes only because the text calls them approximate. No crux flags, no anchors listed (belays are described by ledge or tree). No rappel table.
review.other_findings: Text says the route is better pitched as 20 to 24 pitches and also contains unroped scrambles that stored length excludes. Stored descent_text is null.

pitch_detail.notes: Boulder start onto thin, steep ice. Two bolts lead up to an anchor on a ledge on the climber's left; use a stick clip for the first bolt. The route sits in a major avalanche path, so check conditions.
A line of bolts goes out the steep roof across hanging daggers, on soft, muddy rock. It gets harder as the rock turns more vertical. Ends at a bolted anchor 20 m from the start.
The mixed version (M6) adds bolts to reach the dagger; alternatively follow the ice at WI6 to the trees.

review.changed: Wrote 3 pitches; the text gives a length for pitch 2 from the start, so 20 m may be the cumulative figure from the ground. No rappel table: two rappels on a single 70 m rope, not station by station.
review.other_findings: Text warns of heavy avalanche, rockfall and icefall exposure.
